text: Create, Update, and Notify go a long way, but eventually a flow needs logic that isn't a single built-in action — some calculation, some multi-step sequence, something you'll need again in three other flows next month. Action Designer lets you build that logic once, as a custom reusable action, instead of re-implementing it inside every flow that needs it.

Every custom action has the same three-part shape. Inputs are the data it needs, defined explicitly. Internal steps are the actual logic — built from the same built-in actions you already know, scripting steps for anything that needs real logic, or even IntegrationHub actions. Outputs are the data it hands back once it finishes, usable as a data pill by the calling flow.

A genuinely common example is a custom action called Calculate SLA Due Date. Its input is a priority level. Internally, it runs the business logic mapping priority to a response window and computes the actual due date. Its output is that calculated date, ready to feed into a data pill — logic written correctly once, not re-derived by whoever builds the next flow.

Any flow that needs an SLA due date — an Incident flow, a Change flow, a Service Catalog fulfillment flow — calls this one action instead of re-implementing the date math three separate times, with three separate chances to get it slightly wrong.

If that logic lives in one custom action, fixing a bug or adjusting the business rule means updating it in exactly one place, and every flow that calls it picks up the fix automatically. Copy-paste the same logic into five flows instead, and fixing it means finding and correctly re-editing all five.

Once built, a custom action shows up in the flow action picker right alongside the built-in actions from Lesson 9 — no special syntax, no extra import step. You map its Inputs the same way you'd map any action's fields, and consume its Outputs as data pills the same way.
One action, called everywhere it's needed, fixed in exactly one place. Next up: the Flow Actions Lab, where you'll work through a full written scenario using everything from this chapter.
